full_instruction: Write a historical fiction story about a volunteer nurse working in an overcrowded field hospital during the 1918 influenza pandemic. She keeps a private tally of patient names in the margins of a hymn book, unable to bear a formal ledger of the dead. Set the story during a single thirty-six-hour shift when the hospital runs out of gauze. Write the entire story in present tense to convey the immediacy of the crisis. During the story, reveal that the nurse has been quietly hiding her own influenza symptoms so she can keep working. End with the nurse finally collapsing at her post just as a relief shift arrives.

constraints.requirement: Write a historical fiction story
Protagonist is a volunteer nurse working in an overcrowded field hospital during the 1918 influenza pandemic
She keeps a private tally of patient names in the margins of a hymn book, unable to bear a formal ledger of the dead
Set the story during a single thirty-six-hour shift when the hospital runs out of gauze
Write the entire story in present tense to convey the immediacy of the crisis
Reveal that the nurse has been quietly hiding her own influenza symptoms so she can keep working
End with the nurse finally collapsing at her post just as a relief shift arrives

text:
The wind howls outside the canvas walls and cuts through the tent with a sharpness that feels almost like a needle. Inside, the air smells of antiseptic, sweat, and a faint metallic tang of blood. The field hospital, hastily erected beside a trench line in the Somme valley, is a maze of tents and wooden frames that have been converted into wards for the sick and wounded.

Eleanor “Nell” Whitaker leaves her small town in Massachusetts only weeks earlier, driven by an unshakable sense of duty. The war has already claimed countless lives on the front lines, but now the influenza outbreak is sweeping through the camps like a second, invisible army. She cannot sit idly while soldiers—some with broken limbs, others barely able to stand—suffer from this merciless disease.

On her first day she finds herself in the center of a room that holds twenty patients who are all coughing and wheezing. The nurse in charge, a stern woman named Mary Carter, ushers her around the cramped space, pointing out the layout of beds, the placement of the small water cooler, and the makeshift isolation areas where those with severe symptoms are kept apart from the rest.

“Remember,” Mary says, voice low but urgent, “the influenza is highly contagious. We can’t let it spread among the wounded. Keep your hands clean, keep your distance when you can.”

Nell nods, her hands trembling slightly as she reaches for a fresh pair of gloves. She has never worked in a field hospital before; her training came from a small nursing school in Boston, and she has only ever cared for people in a more orderly setting. The tents are crowded, the staff stretched thin, and every day feels like a battle against time itself.

The first patient Nell attends to is a young lieutenant named Thomas “Tom” Avery, barely twenty‑two, who’s been wounded in a raid earlier that month. His arm lies in a sling, his chest heaving with each cough. He is pale, the color of ash, and his eyes are darkened from lack of sleep.

“Sir,” Nell whispers as she approaches, her voice steady enough to mask her nerves. “I’m Nurse Whitaker. I’ll take care of you.”

Tom manages a weak smile that betrays more fatigue than gratitude. “Thank God you’re here.” He coughs again, a high‑pitched sound that echoes in the tight space. Nell knits beside his bed, carefully placing a clean gauze over his chest before sliding her hand to his arm and checking for swelling.

“You need to rest,” she says softly. “And we’ll keep your temperature checked every hour.”

When she leaves the ward, she notices a small group of men huddled near the entrance of the tent, their eyes wide with fear. The influenza has spread among the ranks like wildfire; many are coughing so violently that they seem to be fighting for each breath.

Later that afternoon, as the sun dips behind the hills and the air grows cooler, Nell is called back into the ward. A new patient has been brought in—an 18‑year‑old nurse from the front who has lost her leg in a shell shock. She lies on a cot with a bandage wrapped around her thigh, her face pale and lined with tears.

“Nell,” she whispers hoarsely. “I… I’m scared.”

Nell sits beside her, placing her hand over the other’s trembling fingers. The nurse’s eyes flick up to meet hers—a look that is both pleading and hopeful. “You’re not alone,” Nell says. “We’re here for you. We’ll get through this together.”

The night falls, and with it comes a new wave of coughing patients—more than the tents can hold. Nell’s shift stretches on, her hands moving from patient to patient in a frantic rhythm that feels almost mechanical. She applies ointments, takes temperatures, delivers whispered words of comfort, and keeps an eye on the charts that track each patient’s pulse and fever.

In the middle of this chaos, a young soldier named Daniel “Danny” O’Connor is brought into the ward. He has been wounded in the front and now faces the flu’s cruel combination with his injuries. His eyes are red‑rimmed from crying; he stares at Nell as if she can save him from the invisible foe.

“Please,” he whispers, voice barely audible over the coughing. “I’m dying.”

Nell understands the fear that clings to those words more than any diagnosis. She takes a deep breath and says, “We’ll do everything we can. You’re stronger than you think.” She checks his pulse—steady but slow—and applies a cool compress on his forehead.

The next morning, as the first rays of sun peek over the horizon, the field hospital’s command staff arrive with new orders. A supply convoy has brought in fresh blankets and a small batch of the latest medicine—a sulfonamide antibiotic that is still experimental but offers hope against secondary bacterial infections.

Eleanor feels her heart lift a little as she watches the medics distribute the supplies. The nurses hurriedly gather the patients who can be moved into new, better‑ventilated tents. She helps arrange the beds, ensuring the isolation wards are set up properly, and instructs the younger nurses on how to handle the new medications.

As the day progresses, Nell sees a pattern emerge—a fragile rhythm between hope and despair. Some patients, like Tom Avery, begin to recover slowly; their coughs lessen, their breaths become steadier. Others, such as Daniel O’Connor, slip further into the abyss of the flu’s relentless grip. In that small tent in the Somme valley, life hangs on a thread.

At night, when the field hospital is quiet and the only sound is the distant rumble of artillery, Nell sits by her own cot, writing in the little notebook she carried from home. She records the names of the patients, their symptoms, and any notes that might help future nurses understand the disease better. She writes a short poem about the bravery of those who served on both sides of the front—a tribute to all the soldiers and nurses who faced an invisible enemy.

The next morning she hears a soft knock at her tent door. A new patient has arrived—Maryann, only fifteen, with a fever that spikes higher than any others they’ve seen. She is the youngest in the ward, and her eyes are wide with terror as she looks around at the crowded tents.

Eleanor’s hands tremble for a moment before she places them on Maryann’s shoulder. “I’m Nurse Whitaker,” she says gently. “We’re going to help you. You’re not alone.”

Maryann manages a shaky smile, and for that brief instant, the cold air seems to soften around them.

In those weeks she learns more than medical skills; she learns resilience, compassion, and an unyielding sense of purpose. The influenza pandemic is relentless, but so are the people who face it—soldiers who fight on the front lines, nurses who tend to the wounded, and volunteers like Nell who step into the chaos with a quiet determination.

When the war finally ends in 1919, Eleanor returns home with a heavy heart but also an unbreakable spirit. The field hospital’s tents have been dismantled, the soldiers’ bodies are buried, and the influenza has left its mark on the world forever. Yet she carries with her stories of courage and humanity that will echo through generations.

The last thing she writes in her notebook before leaving is a simple line: “In every cough, there is hope; in every hand held, there is life.” And as she walks away from the Somme valley, she knows that the memory of those crowded tents and the people who survived inside them will stay with her forever.

---

**The 36‑Hour Shift**

It’s June 12th, 1918. The field hospital has just run low on gauze. Eleanor Whitaker has only just finished her morning rounds, having checked twenty patients and given them their usual morphine and sulfonamide. The day has been a long crawl between coughs that tear at the thin walls of the tents.

She carries a small pouch of gauze—just enough for an emergency wound or two. By noon she’s used it to bandage Lieutenant Thomas Avery’s splintered arm and to patch a small cut on Private James Hall’s leg. A single sheet is enough, but the need for quick, clean dressing in that cramped space means each piece must be spent fast.

By 3 p.m., a sudden flurry of coughing patients bursts into the ward—four more soldiers who’ve been transferred from an even smaller tent because their fever has escalated. Their wounds are deep and bleeding; their lungs are filled with fluid. Nell’s fingers tremble as she tries to keep her breathing steady.

She presses her hand over the gauze pouch, feeling its emptiness. “We’re out,” she whispers to herself. She looks around—no one else seems to notice the shortage. The other nurses are busy with their own patients, and the doctors have gone out for a short break.

The first patient in is Private Samuel O’Neil, who’s been hit by shrapnel on his thigh. His wound is gaping, and blood flows like a slow river down his leg. Nell knits beside him, her heart pounding. She reaches into her pocket for the last sheet of gauze she kept aside for emergencies. The paper crinkles in her palm.

“Sir,” she says softly, “I’m going to do what I can.” She wraps the gauze around his wound with swift, practiced motions—her fingers moving like a seasoned dancer. When she finishes, she ties it tightly with a makeshift string made from an old belt. The wound is covered; the bleeding slows.

The second patient, Private Harold Finch, has a small but painful cut on his hand that won’t stop bleeding. Nell again uses the last sheet of gauze to tie it off. She tells him in a calm voice that she will keep an eye on him and that if the wound worsens she will call for help.

At 5 p.m., a nurse named Mary Carter calls out, “We’re down! No more gauze!” The news spreads like wildfire through the cramped space. A sense of panic sweeps over the ward as they realize the emergency supply has vanished.

Nell turns to her hymnbook—the one she keeps open on her lap, its pages worn and stained from years of use. In the margins beneath a line of “Lord, keep me, my heart is beating,” she writes in quick ink:

> **Gauze shortage** – 5/06

She can feel the weight of that single sheet of gauze as if it were a life itself. The next hour will be about making that one piece stretch and sharing what little is left.

As night falls, the artillery fire grows louder, but inside the tent, the sound is muffled by the canvas walls. The patients’ coughs become ragged; their breaths shallow. Nell can feel the tension in her own chest as she listens to them fight for each breath. She walks from one patient to another, checking vitals and giving words of comfort.

At 7 p.m., a new patient is brought in—a young woman named Anna, only sixteen, with a fever that has been raging since dawn. Her wound on the shoulder is a shallow cut; she is barely breathing. Nell looks at her—her eyes are wide with fear, and her lips tremble. She reaches for the last sheet of gauze, which is now just a thin strip.

“Anna,” Nell whispers, “we’ll do what we can.” She wraps the gauze around Anna’s shoulder wound in a careful, almost reverent motion. The patient’s breathing steadies slightly as the bandage is applied. Nell presses her hand over Anna’s cheek and whispers a short prayer from the hymnbook—“Let there be peace.”

The night grows colder. The wind howls outside, but inside the tent it is still. As she walks back to the central cot where she keeps her hymnbook, she hears a cough that sounds like a dying animal.

It is Private James Hall. His chest has filled with fluid; his breathing is shallow and desperate. Nell knits beside him, her fingers trembling as she takes his pulse—slow but steady. She whispers, “We’re running out of gauze, I’m sorry,” then presses the last remaining piece of gauze onto his chest wound. The wound is small but the bleeding stops.

She writes in the hymnbook’s margin beneath a line of “O Lord, keep them all,”

> **Last gauze** – 8/06

When the first light of dawn breaks over the horizon, the field hospital staff have started to arrive with fresh supplies—new blankets, a small supply of gauze that is enough for ten patients. The doctors return, and the nurses begin to set up new isolation wards.

Eleanor, exhausted but resolute, sits back on her cot as the sun rises higher. She closes her hymnbook gently, its pages creaking like an old door. In the margin, the names of those she has tended are still there—Thomas Avery, Samuel O’Neil, Anna, and James Hall—each with a line of ink that holds their memory.

The next day, when the new gauze arrives, she will open the hymnbook again, write down the names, and place them beside the verses that have carried her through the night. The hymnal is no longer just a book of songs; it has become her private ledger—a silent testament to the lives she could not save but could still remember.

---

**Hiding Her Fever**

She does not tell anyone—no one will believe her or would even dare ask. She hides her own influenza symptoms with a steady, practiced rhythm that keeps her from collapsing on the floor of the ward.

After each patient visit, she squeezes a small glass of water in the back corner of the tent and drinks it slowly while she wipes her sweat‑slick forehead. The coughs that come at night are kept to a minimum; she takes them when no one is looking, swallows the mucus quickly, then returns to the ward. Her chest feels tight, but she forces herself to breathe through it like she would through a wound.

When Mary Carter calls out for gauze and the supplies run low, Nell’s pulse races with both fear and determination. She knows that if her own body fails now, she will not be able to stay on this 36‑hour shift. She whispers silently to herself in the dark: *I must keep working. I cannot let my own sickness stop me.*

Later that night, when the tent is quiet except for a few coughs and the distant artillery, Nell sits at her cot and writes a quick note in the hymnbook margin:

> **Hiding my fever** – 9/06

She does not write it as an admission; she writes it as a reminder to herself that she will be fine if she keeps fighting. The ink is faint but steady, like her own resolve.

The next morning when fresh gauze arrives, Nell’s chest feels lighter, and the coughs ease slightly. She smiles at the thought of how close she had come to collapse in the middle of a patient’s bed. She knows that she will continue to hide her symptoms until the end of the shift because she cannot afford to leave the ward empty when so many depend on her.

The story ends with Eleanor closing the hymnbook, feeling the weight of the names and her own hidden fever. She steps out into the dawn, breathing deeply, ready to face another day where she will keep working even as her body trembles, because the lives she tends are worth every ounce of pain she hides.

And then, just as the relief shift’s first nurse—an exhausted young woman named Grace—steps into the tent and greets her with a tired smile, Nell feels the world tilt. Her chest tightens, her breath catches. The last line of her hidden note in the hymnbook trembles under her fingers: **Hiding my fever** – 9/06.

The air shivers, the canvas creaks, and for one heart‑stopping moment, the nurse collapses at her post—her body giving in to the invisible enemy she has been fighting alone. The relief shift arrives with a sigh of relief, but the quiet that follows is heavy with the knowledge that some battles are won only when the fighters themselves are lost.

full_instruction: Write a mystery story about a train conductor who disappears somewhere between two stations on a night express. The lead investigator on board is a retired detective traveling incognito as an ordinary passenger. Set the story entirely within the train's dining car and narrow sleeping corridors. Write the entire story in first person from the retired detective's point of view. During the story, reveal that the conductor staged his own disappearance to escape a debt owed to one of the passengers. End with the conductor being found hiding inside an unused luggage compartment two cars away.

A train conductor disappears somewhere between two stations on a night express
The lead investigator on board is a retired detective traveling incognito as an ordinary passenger
Set entirely within the train's dining car and narrow sleeping corridors
Write the entire story in first person from the retired detective's point of view
Reveal that the conductor staged his own disappearance to escape a debt owed to one of the passengers
End with the conductor being found hiding inside an unused luggage compartment two cars away

text:
**The Midnight Express: A Dining‑Car Mystery – First Person**

I never thought a night on a train would make me feel so alive again. The old rails beneath my feet hummed like a heartbeat, and the world outside was nothing but cold darkness. I had taken this trip incognito—no badge, no case files, just an old wool coat, a battered hat, and a notebook that held more secrets than any police dossier ever did.

The Midnight Express left Oldtown Station under a sky full of stars, its silver belly cutting through the night like a promise. Inside, the dining car was a world of its own: polished mahogany tables, crystal chandeliers that threw warm light over steaming plates, and passengers who seemed to be living in a bubble separate from the rest of the world.

I sat at the third row, sipping coffee that tasted like burnt wood, listening to an elderly couple laugh about their grandchildren and a young journalist tapping notes on her notebook. The conductor—Thomas Hale—was moving through the dining car with his usual confidence, brass badge glinting in the lantern light as he checked tickets and announced stops. He had been with the railway company for twenty years, and I could tell by the way his green eyes always seemed to look ahead of him.

At 11:47 p.m., a faint hiss cut through the dining car. “Did you hear that?” whispered a passenger in the third row. Thomas turned sharply. The source was a shadow moving across the floorboards toward the narrow sleeping corridor at the end of the dining car—moving faster than any human could.

The conductor’s badge lay on the polished table beside a broken glass bottle, its surface reflecting an unsteady glow. I reached for my radio—a relic from my days in the force—but it crackled with static and then fell silent. The train seemed to hold its breath. Thomas hurried toward the corridor, followed by a small group of passengers who had sensed something off in the air.

The sleeping corridor was a tight, narrow passage lined with doors that opened onto bunks. The lights flickered, casting long shadows along the walls. The train’s horn blew again, echoing through the carriages, but no one noticed it; everyone was drawn toward the anomaly at the end of the dining car.

I stepped ahead, my detective instincts firing. I knew the layout of this corridor intimately—how each door could hide a secret, how the narrowness forced people to look closely. As I passed the first set of doors, I whispered, “Let’s see what you’re hiding.”

The shadow had vanished as quickly as it appeared, but along the corridor’s wall lay an unusual glow—a faint blue light pulsing like a heartbeat on the rail that ran beneath the floorboards. I followed it; my heart quickened.

When I reached the midpoint of the corridor, the lights went out entirely. The train seemed to hold its breath. Only the soft hiss of steam and a faint metallic taste in the air remained. I felt the cold brush of wind as if from nowhere. I heard nothing but my own breathing echoing through the narrow passage.

Suddenly, I felt a chill on my shoulder. A translucent figure—an apparition wearing a conductor’s uniform—slid past me, its jacket made of mist that shimmered in the blue glow. It drifted into the darkness and disappeared, leaving behind only the faint echo of a whistle and an empty brass badge.

Back in the dining car, the passengers were unsettled. The lights flickered again, casting eerie shadows across the tables. Thomas Hale was nowhere to be seen; his badge lay on the floor, its inscription glowing softly: *“Time is a track we all follow.”*

I gathered the passengers in a circle beside the dining car’s central table. I spoke in a calm voice that carried through the quiet hum of the train: “We are in a place where time and space seem to bend. The conductor vanished into thin air between two stations. But we can still find clues.”

I opened my notebook, filled with notes from the night: the exact timing of the hiss, the blue glow’s pattern along the corridor, the broken bottle’s placement, and the inscription on the badge. I examined the rail under the dining car floorboards—its surface rippled where the light touched.

“Let me show you something,” I said, pulling out a small metal detector from my pocket—a relic from my detective days. The device hummed as it scanned the rail. It beeped once, then again, and a faint vibration pulsed through the car. I felt the air shift, as if a hidden mechanism had been triggered.

The train’s engines roared louder, pulling us forward toward the next station. I closed my notebook, pressed the metal detector against the rail, and whispered, “We’ll find out what happened to Thomas Hale before we reach our destination.”

---

### The Truth Unfolds

As the Midnight Express pulled into the next station, a sudden rush of adrenaline hit me—not from danger but from realization. In the silence that followed, I remembered the passenger in the third row who had whispered about the hiss. She was no ordinary traveler; she was Margaret Hargrove, a wealthy widow with a reputation for lending money to anyone who could not pay—an old habit Thomas Hale had known all too well.

I recalled an earlier conversation with Thomas during the journey: he’d been nervous, his hands trembling as he checked his watch. He'd mentioned a debt that “was getting heavier by the mile.” When I asked him about it, he tried to deflect, but something in my tone made him uneasy. The truth was simple and cunning.

Thomas had staged his own disappearance to escape the debt owed to Margaret Hargrove. In the past, she’d lent him a sizable sum of money—one that he could not repay because his earnings as a conductor were modest. When she pressed him for repayment, Thomas saw no way out except disappearing mid‑journey and hoping the authorities would never trace him back.

He had planned it meticulously: leaving his badge on the dining car table beside a broken bottle (the bottle being a prop he’d placed there to create an illusion of a sudden accident). The blue glow was not supernatural at all but a cleverly disguised optical device—an old, small LED array wired into the rail’s underside. When the train slowed near Midway Station, Thomas activated it, causing the lights in the corridor to flicker and the blue glow to appear, drawing everyone’s attention away from his vanishing act.

In the narrow sleeping corridor, he had slipped onto a hidden platform that ran beneath the rails—an abandoned service track that only a few old engineers knew about. From there, he could board an empty freight car that would later be loaded onto a different train heading northbound, leaving no trace of him on the Midnight Express.

---

### The Aftermath

When I finally revealed this to the passengers, their reactions ranged from disbelief to indignation. Margaret Hargrove was stunned; she had expected to find Thomas in custody or at least in an interrogation room. She demanded a full investigation into the train’s conductors and the company’s oversight. The railway officials were quick to distance themselves, stating that they had no knowledge of any disappearance.

I left the train with my notebook full of evidence: photographs of the broken bottle, the brass badge, the blue glow, and my own notes on Thomas’s nervous behavior. I filed a report with the local police and also reached out to Margaret, explaining the situation honestly. She was furious but eventually understood that her debt had led to a man’s desperate escape.

---

### The Final Revelation

Just before the Midnight Express pulled into the terminal at the next major station, an assistant conductor—who had been trailing me from a few carriages back—whispered urgently, “Captain, you need to see this.” He gestured toward a door marked *“Luggage Compartment 5”*.

I followed, heart racing. The doors were stiff, but the key I’d found on the platform earlier slid in with a click. Inside, the compartment was dimly lit by a single bulb that flickered. Rows of old suitcases and trunks lined the walls; the space smelled faintly of cedar and dust.

And there—hiding beneath a stack of discarded coats and an empty suitcase—was Thomas Hale, eyes wide with fear but alive. He had been in this unused luggage compartment for hours, waiting for the train to pass and hoping no one would notice his absence from the passenger list. His hands were trembling, not from the cold but from the realization that his plan was unraveling.

He stared at me, then down at the brass badge he’d left behind, realizing how close he'd come to being caught by coincidence alone. “I—” he began, but I cut him off with a firm hand on my hip.

“I’m not here to arrest you,” I said, “but I am here to bring you back to where you belong—where the law can catch up with your debt.” Thomas’s eyes flickered between relief and fear. He nodded slowly, understanding that his escape was only a brief pause in a longer journey toward accountability.

I escorted him out of the compartment and into the bright daylight of the terminal. Margaret Hargrove met us at the entrance, her face a mask of anger and disbelief. I explained everything: how Thomas had staged his disappearance to avoid paying her debt, how he’d used an old service track and a hidden luggage compartment to hide.

She stared at him for a long moment before she turned back toward me. “You’ve done what most would have left unresolved,” she said softly. “I appreciate your integrity.”

The Midnight Express continued its journey, carrying passengers unaware of the drama behind the dining car lights. For me, it was another case closed—not in the sense of catching a thief or solving a crime—but in unraveling the human motives that drive people to extremes.

Thomas Hale was taken into custody at the terminal. The unused luggage compartment became a reminder of how easily one could slip through the cracks of a moving world, and how, sometimes, it takes a detective’s eye—and an honest heart—to bring them back onto the rails of responsibility.

full_instruction: Write a mystery story about a wartime radio operator who intercepts a coded message that turns out to describe a murder before it happens. She has a talent for cracking ciphers but almost no patience for procedure or her superiors. During the story, reveal that the coded message was sent by the future victim himself, trying to warn someone too late. Set the story inside a cramped underground listening station during a single overnight shift. Write the entire story without using the word "code." End with the operator racing to stop a murder she now believes has already happened somewhere else.

constraints.requirement: Write a mystery story
Protagonist is a wartime radio operator who intercepts a coded message that turns out to describe a murder before it happens
She has a talent for cracking ciphers but almost no patience for procedure or her superiors
Reveal that the coded message was sent by the future victim himself, trying to warn someone too late
Set the story inside a cramped underground listening station
Story takes place during a single overnight shift
Write the entire story without using the word "code"
End with the operator racing to stop a murder she now believes has already happened somewhere else

text:
The night air was a thin, electric hiss that seeped through the damp stone of the bunker and turned the steel walls into a living thing. In the cramped listening station, only twenty feet wide and barely enough room for two people to sit side‑by‑side, the flickering lamps threw shadows like specters on the wall panels covered with patchwork radio dishes and tangled cables.

Evelyn “Evie” Marlowe was alone in that space when the shift began. She had been pulled from her desk at the Admiralty’s cipher office to this underground outpost because of a talent she had cultivated for months—a knack for unraveling patterns that others saw as meaningless noise. The other operators were meticulous, following every protocol and procedure with an almost religious reverence. Evie was not one of them.

She settled into her chair, the leather creaking beneath her, and let the whirring of the radio console settle into a low hum. She was listening for static from the enemy transmissions—an endless stream of encrypted chatter that she could decode in her mind like an invisible melody. Tonight, however, there was something different in the air.

A crackle cut through the background noise. The monitor's screen flickered to life, and a burst of words appeared in a language Evie had never seen before: “Bqf zkh xkqj fzqv htz.” She squinted at the letters, her mind working faster than the rest of the world could keep up with.

The first instinct was to pull out her notebook and jot down the string. But she didn’t have patience for paperwork. Instead, she leaned forward, listening to the transmission as it came in through the speaker, letting the rhythm of the words guide her. She heard a pattern—every third letter seemed to be part of a key phrase.

She started with the first three letters: “Bqf.” In her mind she tried different shifts, then frequency analysis, and finally she remembered a method that had worked for the most stubborn ciphers: taking every second letter from the series. She pulled out her fingers as if they were keys on an old piano and began tapping.

The result was almost too simple to be true. “Bqf” became “Murder.” The rest of the string, when decoded in a similar way, spelled:

“Eve is watching you, we’ll find the killer.”

Her heart hammered against her ribs as she stared at the monitor that had just revealed its secret. She was a radio operator; this was nothing more than intercepted military chatter, not an ominous prophecy. But something about the phrasing felt oddly personal—like it had been written for her.

She tried to keep calm, told herself to stay rational. The rest of the night unfolded as usual: waves of enemy transmissions, the occasional burst of laughter from the other side of the world, and the steady tick of the clock on the wall that marked each minute she’d spent at the desk.

At 3 a.m., after the last transmission had faded into silence, she turned to her supervisor—a man named Captain Harris. He was an old war veteran with a scar across his cheek from a gunshot years ago. He always wore a stiff uniform and had a habit of speaking in clipped sentences that felt like military orders.

“Captain,” Evie said, her voice barely above a whisper, “I think I’ve found something.”

Harris turned, his eyes squinting as if trying to see through the dimness. “What is it?”

“It’s… it’s not a regular transmission.” She gestured at the monitor. The words still glowed faintly on the screen: “Eve is watching you, we’ll find the killer.”

Harris rubbed his forehead, a sign that he was thinking. “I’m listening to what?”

Evie leaned in closer. “The enemy’s signal. I’ve decoded it. It says… it says something about a murder.”

Harris frowned. “That’s nonsense. The enemy doesn’t send personal messages. They’re sending encrypted orders, not riddles.”

She let out a breath that sounded like a sigh. “But the words… they’re clear. Murder, watching you…”

He didn’t look at her for a moment. He pulled up his own notebook and began scribbling down the decoded message in block letters.

“Captain,” she said again, softer now. “This is not just any intercepted transmission. The pattern—”

She held up her hands to keep him from reading too far ahead. “It’s from someone who knows me. It sounds like it could be a warning.”

Harris sighed and pushed his glasses back onto the bridge of his nose. “If this is a prank, you’re wasting everyone’s time. If it’s real, I’ll need you to report it to headquarters.” He pressed the button on his radio and sent a message up to their chain of command.

She didn’t have time for that. The night was still deep, and she could hear faint footsteps in the corridor outside the station—footsteps of a guard making his rounds. Her mind kept racing with possibilities: a murderer, an enemy spy, or even a supernatural trickster.

She started to go through her own knowledge of the patterns used by the enemy for encryption. She knew that certain letters were more frequent than others, and she began to look at each letter in the intercepted string as if it was a puzzle piece. The realization hit her like a bolt: the message had been transmitted using a method she’d employed for years—one that involved taking every other letter.

She whispered under her breath, “Murder Eve is watching you… we’ll find the killer.” Her eyes widened; the words were now a sentence rather than a set of disjointed phrases. It was almost as if someone had written it directly into her mind.

The guard’s footsteps grew louder and then faded away again. The station’s air was still, the hum of the radio equipment steady as a metronome. She felt an odd sense of calm that she hadn’t known existed in her chest—like the world had shifted from a battlefield to a personal chess match where she was both player and spectator.

She pressed the button on the monitor and began typing into her notebook, trying to keep up with the rhythm of the words as they flowed through her mind. She realized she wasn’t decoding a message for an enemy; she was decoding something else entirely. The words seemed to be speaking to her directly: “Eve is watching you.” It almost felt like a warning from someone who knew her too well.

She remembered a story her grandmother had told her when she was young—a tale of a man who lived in the future and sent messages back through time, trying to alter events that were already set. She’d laughed at it then, but now the words on the monitor seemed to echo that very story.

Her heart pounded against her ribs as she realized that the message might not be an enemy tactic but a warning from someone who had somehow found a way to send information back in time. And the only person who could interpret such a strange transmission was her, because of her unique talent for finding meaning where others saw only noise.

She let out a breath and looked up at the ceiling, where the faint light flickered like distant stars. “What if this is the future victim?” she whispered to herself. “If he’s sending a warning—he can’t do anything about it. He’s already dead.”

The words on the screen began to shift; she felt her fingers moving as though guided by an invisible hand.

“Evie, you’re not listening!” Captain Harris’s voice cut through the silence, sharp and urgent. “You’ve been on this station all night. You’re going insane.”

She turned toward him. “Captain, I’m telling you that there’s a message in the transmission that isn’t from the enemy. It’s a warning about a murder that will happen tonight—at least according to what the future victim says.”

Harris stared at her for a long moment. He could see the desperation in her eyes, and his own face softened as he remembered how close he had been to death in the last war.

“Okay,” he said quietly, “but you’re going to follow protocol. We can’t just leave this to you.”

Evie nodded, but she was already moving toward the door, her mind racing with possibilities of who could be targeted and where the murder would occur. The bunker’s doors were locked from the outside, but there was a small hatch that led into the tunnels below. She could hear faint voices down in the tunnel—her own voice echoing off the walls as she whispered to herself.

She slipped out of the station, her boots making soft clicks on the stone floor. The air grew cooler as she descended the narrow staircase. The world outside was a dark maze of earth and stone, lit only by her flashlight that cast long, wavering shadows.

When she reached the bottom, she heard voices—soft, hurried. She followed them to an abandoned section of the tunnel where a small group of soldiers were huddled together. Their eyes flicked toward her as she entered, but no one shouted or warned her to stay back. It was clear that she had stumbled into a hidden area used for covert operations.

One of the men—an older soldier with a scar across his cheek—turned at her and asked in a low voice, “What are you doing here?”

Evie didn’t answer; instead, she pulled out the notebook from her pocket. She flipped it open to the page where the decoded message was written: “Murder Eve is watching you… we’ll find the killer.”

She held it up between them. The soldier stared at the words as if they were a revelation.

“This… this is an order from someone.” He whispered, looking at her and then at the other soldiers. He nodded slowly to himself and turned back toward the dark corridor.

Evie felt the weight of something she couldn’t quite explain. She was no longer just a radio operator; she was a messenger between times. The message had come from the future victim himself, trying to warn someone too late.

She realized that if she could only get this warning to the right person before the murder happened, perhaps she could stop it. But the world had already been set in motion, and there were no guarantees that her interference would change anything. She felt a cold determination settle over her: if she didn’t act now, someone else would die.

She looked back at the soldiers, then turned toward the tunnel’s exit. The path out of the underground station led to the city above—a city that was still alive and moving with its own secrets.

The last thing she saw before stepping into the light outside was the echoing footfalls of a guard from the bunker behind her, and the faint sound of someone whispering: “Eve is watching you.”

Her phone rang as she stepped onto the stone steps. She answered it without hesitation, knowing that the future victim’s warning had already been received by someone in the wrong place.

She turned to run—her legs moved faster than they ever had before, her mind racing with every possible route to stop a murder that seemed to have already happened somewhere else. The underground listening station behind her hummed like an old heartbeat as she sprinted toward whatever darkness lay ahead.

text:
The air inside the canvas tent doesn’t smell like the countryside anymore. It smells of carbolic acid, unwashed skin, and the sweet, heavy rot of fever.

Elara presses a handkerchief over her mouth, though it does little to filter the humidity of three hundred breathing bodies crammed into a space designed for fifty. It is October 1918, and the "Spanish Flu" has turned the village of Oakhaven into a staging ground for a silent, invisible war.

She is a volunteer—a schoolteacher by trade, a daughter of a carpenter by birth—but here, she is merely a ghost in a white apron. Her hands are raw, the skin cracked and weeping from constant scrubbing in basins of lye and water. 

A sharp, jagged spike of heat pierces her skull, making her vision swim for a heartbeat. She blinks it away, forcing her posture upright. She cannot afford to falter.

"Next!" she calls out, her voice cracking.

A young man, no older than twenty, is carried in on a litter. His face is a terrifying shade of plum, his eyes rolled back into his head. He is gasping, his chest heaving in a rhythmic, terrifying shudder.

"He’s burning up," a soldier cries out, his uniform torn. He drops the litter onto the straw-covered floor. "He won't stop coughing."

Elara moves with a practiced, mechanical grace. She doesn't have time for the luxury of hesitation. She takes a basin of cool water and a cloth, dabbing at his forehead. She needs to bring the temperature down before his lungs seize completely. Every movement feels like she is wading through chest-deep molasses, her muscles heavy and unresponsive. 

"Easy, son," she whispers, though she doesn't know his name. "Just breathe. Just follow my lead."

Around her, the hospital is a symphony of agony. The rhythmic *thump-thump* of a percussionive cough echoes from every corner. The high-pitched wail of a mother in the far corner is cut short by a wet, rattling sound that makes Elara’s stomach turn. This is the "blue death"—the cyanosis that turns the skin a bruised indigo as the lungs fill with fluid.

She moves from bed to bed, a weaver of small comforts in a tapestry of misery. She gives water to the thirsty, who drink with a desperate, greedy intensity. She folds blankets for the shivering. She holds the hands of the dying, squeezing them until their grip loosens and their breath finally stilled.

By dusk, the lanterns are lit, casting long, dancing shadows against the canvas walls. Elara sits on a crate in the corner, her legs trembling with exhaustion. She pulls a small, battered notebook from her apron pocket. She tries to write, but her hand shakes too much.

*October 14th,* she tries to pen. *The numbers are climbing. We lost six more today. The men from the bakery. The girl from the mill. They come in with fire in their blood and leave with ice in their veins.*

She stops. A sudden, violent shudder racks her frame, and she has to press her forehead against the cool wood of the crate to keep from collapsing. Her chest feels tight, a dull ache blooming behind her ribs with every inhale. She swallows hard, tasting the metallic tang of blood in the back of her throat. 

She can’t write about the deaths. She wants to write about the way the young man from the litter looked at her for a fleeting second—a moment of lucidity where he had gripped her wrist and whispered, *“Please, don’t let me be alone.”*

She has stayed. She has held his hand until the very last shudder.

A sudden, violent coughing fit erupts from the cot beside her. A woman, thin and grey, sits up, her eyes wide with terror. "Is it over?" she wheezes. "Am I going?"

Elara stands up, her joints aching. She wipes her face with a damp rag and steps toward the woman. She feels a wave of dizziness so profound she has to grip the edge of the cot to stay upright. She forces a smile, though it feels like a mask of porcelain. She doesn't have medicine to give her, and she doesn't have a miracle to offer. All she has is her presence.

She takes the woman’s hand. It is searing hot.

"Not yet," Elara says, her voice steady despite the hollow ache in her chest. "You’re still here. And I’m right here with you."

Outside, the wind howls through the trees, carrying the scent of fallen leaves. Inside, the lanterns flicker, and the long, grueling night begins again. Elara adjusts her apron, takes a breath of the medicinal air—which feels increasingly like smoke in her lungs—and steps back into the fray.

***

The thirty-six-hour shift begins with a gray, oppressive dawn. 

By the time Elara takes her first watch, the humidity has reached a point where the air feels like a wet shroud. The hospital is at capacity, the tents straining against the wind as if trying to collapse under the weight of the suffering within.

"We’re out," the head nurse, a woman named Miller whose face has become a permanent mask of exhaustion, says as she walks past Elara. Her voice is flat, devoid of any inflection.

Elara pauses, a basin of water in her hands. The world tilts dangerously to the left. She closes her eyes for three seconds, counting to three, then rights herself. "Out of what?"

"Gauze. Cotton bandages. Everything." Miller doesn't stop. "The supply wagon was diverted to the front lines. They say the casualties there are worse. We have to make do."

The news hits Elara like a physical blow. Gauze is the barrier between the living and the rot. It is what holds the pressure on a chest wound, what soaks up the fever-sweat, what covers the weeping sores of the skin. Without it, the work will become visceral, raw, and unbearable.

For the first twelve hours, they improvise. Elara finds herself tearing strips of old bedsheets, boiling them in lye and water, and drying them on the tent poles. It is a frantic, desperate economy of fabric. She watches the men—the soldiers and the local laborers—as they tear at the hems of their own shirts to provide bandages for the neighbors they have carried in from the streets.

By the eighteen-hour mark, the exhaustion begins to settle into Elara’s bones like lead. Her hair feels heavy with sweat, and her eyes burn from the constant sting of carbolic acid. 

A young woman, barely more than a child, is brought in from the village. She has a jagged tear in her arm from a fall, the wound angry and weeping.

"Please," the girl’s mother sobs, clutching Elara’s apron. "She’s bleeding so much."

Elara looks at the meager pile of boiled cloth. It isn't enough. She has to use a long strip of linen, wrapping it tight around the girl's arm, her hands shaking. She has to hold it in place with her own weight for nearly an hour because there are no more ties left. 

"Hold her hand," Elara commands a passing volunteer. "Don't let her move."

The girl’s screams are muffled by the constant roar of the ward—the coughing, the moaning, the frantic whispers of the dying. Elara feels a hot tear track through the grime on her cheek. She can’t use the proper dressings. She can’t provide the sterile comfort the girls deserve. She is fighting a war with nothing but rags and a prayer.

At the twenty-four-hour mark, the "Blue Death" takes a heavy toll. The wards are filled with the sound of labored breathing—the *rattle* that signals the end.

Elara sits in the corner for five minutes, her back against a support pole. Her hands are shaking so violently she has to tuck them into her apron. She pulls out the hymn book.

The margins are getting crowded. The ink is beginning to bleed from the pressure of her frantic writing.

*Henry Vance. Age 34. Died of the fever.*
*Sarah Jenkins. Age 12. The smallest one of all.*

She looks at the names. They are a litany of the discarded. She feels a sudden, terrifying urge to scream, to howl at the injustice of it all—that they are being left to rot in a field while the world turns its back.

She feels a sudden, sharp constriction in her chest, as if an invisible hand is squeezing her lungs. She gasps, a small, wet sound, and quickly covers it with her sleeve. Her head throbs with a rhythmic, pounding heat. *Not yet,* she tells herself, a mantra against the rising tide of her own failing strength. *I cannot leave them.*

She stands up, her knees popping, and walks back into the center of the storm.

The final twelve hours are a blur of gray and shadow. The lanterns burn low, casting flickering orange light over the faces of the dying. There are no more bandages. There is only the water, the cloth, and the constant, rhythmic movement of Elara’s hands.

She spends the final hours of her shift moving from cot to cot, pressing cool, damp rags to foreheads, whispering words of comfort that she hopes reach the ears of the drifting souls. She becomes a weaver of shadows, stitching together the final moments of strangers with nothing but her presence.

When the sun finally rises on the thirty-sixth hour, the light is a pale, sickly yellow.

Elara collapses onto a crate near the entrance. Her muscles are screaming, her skin feels like it is being pulled tight over her ribs, and her throat is raw from talking and weeping. 

She reaches into her apron and pulls out the hymn book. Her fingers are too tired to hold the pen, but she traces the names one last time.

*Julian Thorne.*

The ink is still wet.

She closes her eyes, and for a moment, the smell of carbolic acid and rot fades. She sees the faces of the people in the margins. They aren't data points. They aren't "mortalities."

They are the people she held. And in the silence of the morning, she is the only one who remembers them.

A sudden, sharp crack of a door opening breaks the silence. A group of weary women enter, carrying fresh basins and stacks of linen. They see the heap of white fabric and the slumped figure on the crate. 

"Elara?" one calls out, her voice filled with concern.

Elara doesn't hear her. Her head falls forward, her chin hitting her chest, her body finally surrendering to the weight of the fever and the crushing toll of the night. She falls sideways off the crate, sinking into the straw as the first of the new shift reaches out to catch her.

full_instruction: Write a historical fiction story about a monastery scribe illuminating a manuscript while plague spreads through the surrounding countryside. He has a private habit of hiding small personal sketches in the margins where the abbot will never look closely. text:
The vellum was cool beneath Brother Thomas’s fingers, a smooth, ivory expanse that felt like the only steady thing left in a world dissolving into rot. In the scriptorium of Saint Jude’s, the air remained thick with the scent of linseed oil, crushed lapis lazuli, and the underlying, metallic tang of dying men. Outside the arched windows, the valley of Aethelgard was being swallowed by a grey veil of mist and the frantic tolling of the bell—a rhythmic, mourning pulse that never seemed to cease.

The gates of the monastery had been barred for twenty days, sealed against the Great Mortality that ravaged the countryside. Inside, the scriptorium had become a pressurized vessel of prayer, ink, and claustrophobic devotion. The monastery was no longer a sanctuary for the living; it was a fortress for the dying, and the scriptorium served as its nerve center. The atmosphere was one of suffocating focus. The usual rhythm of the monastery—the ringing of the bells, the movement of the cooks, the laughter of the novices—had been replaced by a singular, haunting sound: the scratching of quills. It was a collective labor of desperation, as if by illuminating the holy words, the brothers could weave a net to catch the falling souls of the valley.

Brother Thomas sat in the same chair he had occupied since the first heavy bolt was slid into place. He was working on the *Codex of Grace*, a masterpiece intended for the altar of the High Bishop. His task was the illumination of the "Passage of Deliverance."

*“For the soul that seeks the light,”* he wrote in a flowing, disciplined Gothic script, *“shall find the gate unbarred.”*

He paused, his hand trembling slightly. A cough erupted from the dormitory—a wet, racking sound that ended in a strangled gasp. Thomas closed his eyes. He saw the faces of the village children in his mind’s eye, their skin turning the color of bruised plums, their eyes clouding over as the plague claimed them.

He turned to his palette. He needed the gold.

He took a small muller and began to grind the aurum leaf. The friction created a warmth in his palms. He worked with a frantic, almost desperate precision. If the world was ending, he reasoned, it must at least be beautiful. If the bodies in the village were being piled like cordwood in the pits, then these pages would be the only things left that were holy.

He began to paint the border. He laid down a deep ultramarine, derived from crushed stones brought from the East. It was the color of the deepest ocean, the color of the veil between life and death. Around the central text, he spiraled vines of ivy and lilies. The lilies were white, pure as a virgin’s breath, their petals tipped with a faint touch of crimson—a reminder of the blood that watered the earth.

Yet, as his brush danced across the vellum, his mind wandered to the hidden appendices of the *Codex*. Tucked between the liturgical prayers and the stories of the saints were the "Compendia of the Healing Hand"—ancient, dusty recipes for poultices, distillations of willow bark, and tinctures of wormwood. They were texts of science disguised as miracles, a treasury of knowledge that the monastery had guarded for centuries.

Beneath the desk, hidden in a hollowed-out stone where the dust lay thickest, Thomas kept a stack of thin, discarded scraps of parchment.

With a steady hand, he began his true work.

While the other brothers focused on the grandeur of the illumination, Thomas used the margins of his own mind to translate the complex medical formulas into a simplified script. He worked in the shadows of the afternoon, when the light was too dim for the Abbot to peer over his shoulder. He copied the proportions of the fever-reducers, the precise measurements of the vinegar-soaks, and the instructions for the cooling wraps.

He was not merely a scribe of the Word; he was a smuggler of life.

Every few days, he would press these scraps into the lining of his heavy woolen habit. He would walk the perimeter of the scriptorium, his face a mask of pious sorrow, until he reached the laundry bins near the postern gate. There, he would slip a few scraps to the sisters who were tasked with carrying the linens to the village—the only ones who could risk the trek through the mist.

Brother Malachi, the elderly cellarer, appeared at Thomas’s shoulder. His face was sunken, his eyes rimmed with red exhaustion. He looked worse than he had in the first week; his skin had taken on a waxy, translucent sheen.

“The fever has reached the infirmary,” Malachi whispered, his voice a dry husk. “They are taking the brothers from the scriptorium one by one. The silence in the dormitory is... it is heavy, Thomas.”

Thomas did not look up from the *Codex of Grace*. He could not afford to. If he looked at Malachi’s face, he would see the end of the world. “Write the Word, Malachi,” he said, his voice raspy from disuse. “The Word is the only thing that does not rot.”

“Is it?” Malachi asked, his voice barely a thread of sound. He looked at the page Thomas was working on—a sprawling, magnificent illumination of a celestial garden. “I see the gold. I see the blue. But I also see the shadows in the corners. I see the way the ink runs when the humidity rises. Is it enough to hold back the Great Mortality?”

Thomas finally paused. He looked at his hands. They were stained permanently with indigo and ochre, the skin cracked and dry. “It is not supposed to hold it back,” he said softly. “It is supposed to be there when it is over. It is the only thing that will remain when the plague has finished its meal.”

He turned back to the vellum. The isolation of the scriptorium was absolute. They were a group of ghosts haunting a house of stone, producing a miracle of light in a season of shadow.

He felt the weight of the isolation most acutely in the late hours. When the candles burned low and the scriptorium fell into a heavy, expectant silence, the walls seemed to pulse. He could hear the distant, rhythmic thud of a hammer from the courtyard—someone reinforcing the gates, or perhaps a funeral pyre being prepared.

It was in these hours that Thomas sought his secret rebellion.

He reached into the deep pocket of his woolen habit and pulled out a small, charcoal stick—a contraband item he had smuggled from the village market weeks ago. He also pulled out a scrap of discarded parchment, a piece of scrap vellum that had been trimmed from a larger sheet.

With a quick, practiced motion, he moved the *Codex of Grace* slightly to the left, positioning it so the shadow of his own shoulder obscured the lower right corner of the page.

He began to draw.

It was not a saint. It was not a martyr. It was a memory.

In the cramped margin, hidden beneath the sweeping tail of the letter *'G'*, Thomas sketched the silhouette of a willow tree by the river outside the monastery walls. It was a tree he had seen in his youth, before the vows, before the silence. He drew the way the branches bowed toward the water, heavy with the weight of the summer heat.

Then, he added a small figure—a girl in a simple linen kirtle, her hair escaping from a braid, sitting on the bank and reading a book of her own. He did not give her a face; he did not need to. He drew the way her shoulders relaxed, the way she seemed to lean into the world as if it were a warm hearth.

It was a forbidden thing—a sketch of longing. It was a rebellion of the heart against the monochrome devotion of the scriptorium.

He worked with a frantic, hushed intensity. The charcoal left a faint grey smudge, a ghost of a life he had left behind. He wanted to capture the way the light hit the water—not the divine light of the *Codex*, but the mundane, fleeting light of a Tuesday afternoon in a world that had not yet turned to ash.

A heavy footfall sounded in the corridor.

Thomas froze. His heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped bird. The Abbot.

He held his breath, his lungs burning. He watched as the Abbot’s shadow fell across the desk, a long, distorted shape that swallowed the gold leaf and the ultramarine. The old man moved closer. The scent of incense and old dust preceded him.

The Abbot leaned over the *Codex*, his withered hand reaching out to trace the gold leaf on the "Passage of Deliverance." Thomas felt a bead of sweat roll down his temple. He kept his hands flat on the desk, concealing the charcoal. He watched the old man’s eyes. They were clouded with age, searching the page for the holiness he demanded.

The Abbot’s gaze swept over the vibrant blue, the shimmering gold, and the intricate, looping letters. He lingered for a second on the bottom right corner—the very spot where the willow tree hid in the shadows.

Thomas felt his pulse leap into his throat. *He sees it. He sees the treason of the tree.*

The Abbot’s face remained a mask of stone. He sighed, a sound of weary approval. “The craftsmanship is... adequate. The blue is deep, like the robes of the martyrs.”

He straightened his back, his joints popping in the silence. “Continue. The Bishop expects the first five folios by the feast of St. Anne.”

He turned and walked away, his heavy robes sweeping the floor.

Thomas sat in the silence that followed, his hand still trembling. He did not look at the sketch. He did not look at the gold. He simply sat in the dark, his thumb tracing the hidden curve of a willow branch, a secret sanctuary of ink and charcoal in a world of dying light.

He reached for his quill and dipped it into the gold.

*“For the soul that seeks the light,”* he wrote, the gold leaf shimmering like a spark in the dying fire.

He worked until his eyes burned and his fingers went numb, a scribe in a tomb, painting a heaven that he knew, with every fiber of his being, he would never see. But for now, in the silence of the sealed gates, the gold was enough.

Weeks later, as the frost began to bite into the stone of the scriptorium, the Abbot returned to Thomas’s station. The village had fallen silent, the gates finally opened to let the dead be burned, and a heavy, hollow peace had settled over the monastery. 

The Abbot stood behind Thomas, his presence as heavy as the history of the walls. He did not speak. His eyes, sharp despite their age, were not on the gilded *Codex*, but on the small, unassuming pile of scraps tucked beneath the desk—the ones Thomas had forgotten to hide in his exhaustion.

The Abbot reached out, his trembling fingers lifting a single piece of parchment. On it, in a hurried, unrefined hand, were the instructions for a willow-bark distillation to break a fever. It was a heresy of sorts—the mingling of the medicinal with the sacred, the secular utility of the monastery's secret knowledge.

Thomas felt the air leave his lungs. He braced for the rebuke, for the stripping of his habit, for the brand of the sinner. He waited for the words that would condemn his theft of the Word for the sake of the flesh.

But the Abbot did not speak. 

He looked at the recipe, then he looked at Thomas. In the old man's eyes, Thomas saw not judgment, but a profound, terrible weariness. The Abbot saw the girl by the willow, the sparrow in the margin, and the desperate, secret mercy of the smuggler. He saw a man who was trying to build a bridge across the abyss with nothing but ink and a heavy heart.

The Abbot’s hand remained steady. He did not crumple the paper. He did not call for the guards. He simply placed the scrap back onto the desk, his fingers lingering for a fraction of a second on the rough vellum.

“The fever is a heavy burden, Brother Thomas,” the Abbot said, his voice barely a whisper that seemed to carry the weight of the valley. “It is a mercy that some of us still remember how to carry it.”

Then, the old man turned and walked away, leaving Thomas alone in the flickering light, the secret of the gold and the secret of the medicine held in a fragile, holy silence.

full_instruction: Write a historical fiction story about a court clerk recording testimony during the Salem witch trials of 1692. During the story, reveal that the clerk has been quietly leaving out certain accusations he believes are false before submitting his transcripts to the magistrates. He keeps his own private set of notes hidden beneath the floorboards of his study at home. Set the story during a single tense day of testimony inside the crowded meetinghouse. Do not use the word "witch" anywhere in the text. End with the clerk burning his private notes the night before the next round of trials begins.

constraints.requirement: Write a historical fiction story
Protagonist is a court clerk recording testimony during the Salem witch trials of 1692
Reveal that the clerk has been quietly leaving out certain accusations he believes are false before submitting his transcripts to the magistrates
He keeps his own private set of notes hidden beneath the floorboards of his study at home
Set the story during a single tense day of testimony inside the crowded meetinghouse
Do not use the word "witch" anywhere in the text
End with the clerk burning his private notes the night before the next round of trials begins

text:
The ink was the first thing to fail me. It wouldn't flow from the quill, thick and stubborn as if the very atmosphere of the courtroom had turned to sludge.

I dipped the nib again, my fingers trembling against the rough wood of the clerk’s desk. Outside, the Massachusetts autumn had turned teeth-cold, but inside the meeting house, the air was heavy with a different kind of frost—a suffocating, feverish heat born of collective hysteria.

My name is Thomas Thorne, and I am a man of letters, a man of record. My duty is to be the conduit of truth, to translate the jagged edges of human experience into the smooth, orderly lines of the law. But as I sat in the shadows of the gallery, watching the proceedings of the Court of Oyer and Terminer, I felt my soul fraying like a worn rope.

"Speak, Goody Proctor," the Magistrate commanded. His voice was like the cracking of dry timber.

I braced my hand. The quill scratched across the parchment.

*“It was in the shape of a black hound,”* the woman sobbed, her face a mask of terror. *“It had eyes like burning coals and it sat upon my breast, choking the breath from my lungs while the shadows danced upon the rafters.”*

I paused, my nib hovering. I looked at the woman. She was a weaver, her hands gnarled from years of work. Was she truly seeing a beast? Or was she seeing the manifestation of a village curdled by fear? My duty was to record her words, not to judge their veracity. Yet, the more I wrote, the more the words felt like stones being piled upon a tomb.

*“The Devil spoke through the girl,”* she continued, her voice rising to a shriek. *“He whispered of the woods, of the pact, of the blood spilled in the name of the Unholy!”*

I felt a bead of sweat roll down my spine. I looked toward the accused—a young woman named Abigail Williams. She sat in the dock, her face pale as moonlight. She didn't look like a conduit for the Enemy; she looked like a child drowning in a sea of her own making. She watched the weaver with a strange, predatory intensity.

The court roared. The neighbors leaned forward, their faces twisted in expressions of pious agony. They wanted the confession. They wanted the name. They wanted the catharsis of the pyre.

I felt the familiar, heavy weight of my secret. Under the desk, hidden by the long skirts of the spectators, lay a secondary set of papers—my "corrections."

As the weaver shrieked about "the pact of blood," my hand moved with a deliberate, practiced grace. I wrote the words as she spoke them, allowing the hysteria to fuel the official record. But in the quiet moments between the Magistrate’s queries, when the court took a breath to gasp for air, I worked with a different kind of focus.

I had begun this clandestine labor weeks ago. I realized that if I recorded every frantic, impossible accusation—the claims of spectral birds, the imaginary marks on skin, the impossible flights through the air—I was providing the fuel for the executioner’s fire. I was crafting a roadmap for destruction.

So, I became a thief of words.

*“The girl claimed I flew over the church,”* the weaver cried out, her eyes rolling back.

I recorded the scream, but when I transcribed the specificities of the "flight" into the final draft for the Magistrate’s review that evening, I softened the blade. I omitted the descriptions of the girl's supposed shapeshifting into a cat. I struck through the specific dates of the "sabbath" meetings that had no basis in geography. I removed the most lurid, nonsensical adjectives—the "stench of brimstone" and the "whispers of the pit"—leaving only the barest, most mundane descriptions of distress.

It was a dangerous game. If I were caught, I would be accused of tampering with the Divine Record. I would be hanged alongside the damned. But as I watched the Magistrate lean in, hungry for more "proof," I felt a desperate, subversive purpose. I was trying to starve the fire. By stripping away the supernatural flourishes, I hoped to leave the court with a record of a woman who was simply... unwell. A woman who was frightened. A woman who was not a monster.

"Does she confess?" the Magistrate demanded, his gavel striking the block with a thud that echoed in my very marrow.

*“I confess!”* the weaver cried out, collapsing into her seat. *“I confess I have seen the Mark! I confess the shadows have claimed me!”*

I recorded the words. I watched the Magistrate nod, his face a portrait of grim righteousness. I watched the guards move in to secure her.

The afternoon stretched on, a grueling marathon of accusation. One by one, more were brought forth. The crowd pressed against the pews, their breath hot and damp. Every time a name was uttered—Sarah Good, Rebecca Nurse—a ripple of weeping or shouting moved through the assembly. 

By the time the sun began to dip below the horizon, casting long, distorted shadows across the floorboards, my hand was cramped into a permanent claw. My wrist ached with a dull, throbbing heat. I looked back at the pages I had filled. They were a chronicle of a village devouring itself, but they were also a lie—a curated, sanitized version of the truth I had witnessed.

I saw the names: Sarah Good, Sarah Osburn, Rebecca Nurse. Names that were once neighbors, friends, mothers. Now, they were merely entries in a ledger of damnation.

I stood to leave, my legs feeling heavy as if I were wading through deep water. As I packed my inkwell, I caught my reflection in a small, distorted mirror hanging near the door. I looked older. My eyes were rimmed with red, and my face was gaunt.

I realized then that my role was not what I had thought. I was not merely a recorder of truth. I was an architect of memory. Every word I transcribed became a brick in the wall of history. If I wrote that she was an enemy of God, she would be an enemy forever in the eyes of the world. If I wrote that she was a victim of a fevered mind, the record might be different.

But the law demanded the first. The law demanded the fear. And I, in my small, trembling rebellion, was trying to steal the fear back, one omitted word at a time.

I stepped out into the biting night air. The wind howled through the leafless trees, sounding hauntingly like the screams I had spent the day transcribing. I looked down at my hands. They were stained black with ink—a permanent mark that would not wash away.

I had recorded the testimony of a dying town. And as I walked toward my home, I knew that while I had survived the day, a part of me would remain in that meeting house, trapped forever in the ink, watching the shadows dance upon the rafters.

***

The sanctuary of my home was a different sort of silence. Here, the walls did not press in with the judgment of the magistrates, and the air did not smell of wet wool and unwashed terror. Yet, I could not find rest. The images of the weaver’s face—the way her eyes rolled back as she spoke of the hound—haunted my sleep.

I retreated to my study, a room that smelled of old paper and cedar. I sat at my private desk, the one where I did not have to pretend for the eyes of the state. 

With a trembling hand, I reached for a loose floorboard beneath my heavy oak chair. I pried it up, the wood groaning in protest, and reached into the dark cavity beneath. 

I pulled out a bundle of papers, bound in a simple leather thong. These were my true records. 

In these pages, there were no omissions. Here, I wrote the truth of the weaver's screams—the graphic details of the "hound," the specific, terrifying names of the "shadows," and the exact, impossible descriptions of the Devil’s pact. I recorded every hallucination, every fever-dream, and every lie told by Abigail Williams. 

I wrote them down in a frantic, jagged script that looked nothing like my steady clerk’s hand. I recorded the lies so that they would never be forgotten, even as I scrubbed them from the official transcripts to save the lives of the accused. 

I was a man of two books: one that served the law, and one that served the truth. 

I dipped my quill into a small pot of ink—the only ink I felt I could trust—and began to write the words the Magistrate would never see. I wrote the names of the monsters, not the ones in the woods, but the ones in the pews. I wrote the names of the innocent, ensuring that when the fires were finally extinguished and the history of this dark year was written, there would be a secret ledger, hidden beneath the floorboards, to tell of what truly happened in the shadows of the meeting house.

But tonight, the air in the room felt different. The weight of the secret had become a physical pressure on my chest, a suffocating heat that matched the fever of the courtroom. I looked at the bundle—the raw, bleeding truth of a community’s madness. I knew that if these papers were ever found, they would be my death warrant. They would be seen as evidence of my own heresy, my own subversion of the Divine Order.

I could not let them exist. I could not be the man who kept the secrets of the dead while the living were being consumed.

I took the bundle to the hearth. 

The fire was already roaring, a hungry orange beast devouring the logs of the previous day. I held the papers over the flames. I watched as the first page curled, the ink of my frantic handwriting bubbling and vanishing. I watched the names of the innocent—the names I had tried to protect by erasing their crimes from the official record—turn into grey flakes of ash.

I watched the graphic descriptions of the hound and the pact vanish into smoke. I watched the evidence of the girl's lies disappear into the heat. 

One by one, the pages succumbed. The heat scorched my face, but I did not flinch. I watched the truth of the meeting house dissolve into nothingness, leaving behind only a pile of white dust and a handful of scorched paper.

The fire consumed it all.

I sat in the darkness of the study, the only light coming from the glowing embers in the grate. The room was empty of my secrets. The floorboard remained open, a hollow mouth in the wood, but it held nothing.

Outside, the wind continued to howl, and in the distance, the bells began to toll. The next round of trials would begin at dawn. The magistrates would have their sanitized records, the law would have its orderly lines, and I would have my silence. I had saved their lives by erasing their voices, and now, I had saved my soul by erasing the record of my own.
